question: A host runs an app behind NGINX on 443 (TLS, auth, IP filtering) plus a management tool bound directly to 9443, and the Security Group allows 9443 from 0.0.0.0/0. What is the management tool's actual security posture?
choices: Protected — NGINX runs on the host, so it filters all HTTP traffic entering the instance regardless of port
Exposed to the entire internet — NGINX only governs ports it serves, so 9443 traffic reaches the tool directly with none of NGINX's controls applied
Protected — the Security Group is stateful, so unsolicited inbound connections are blocked automatically
Exposed only to clients that can complete a TLS handshake against the tool's own certificate
explanation: The Security Group and NGINX are gates in series, and NGINX guards only the ports it actually listens on — a port the SG opens that NGINX doesn't proxy is an unguarded door straight to whatever is bound there. Traffic to 9443 never touches NGINX, so its TLS policy, auth, and allow/deny rules simply don't apply; and 'stateful' means allowed inbound connections get their return traffic automatically — it doesn't block connections the rules explicitly permit. TLS on the tool itself encrypts the channel but authenticates nobody. The fix is one of two moves: restrict 9443 at the SG, or route the tool through NGINX — never leave an open port pointing at an unguarded service.

question: Migrating from a single EC2 host (NGINX at the edge) to ECS behind an ALB, a team copies their VPN-only block for /admin — allow 10.8.0.0/24; deny all; — into the per-task NGINX config. After cutover, every /admin request is denied, including from the VPN. Why, and where must the rule live now?
choices: The task's security group now admits traffic only from the ALB's security group, which rewrites the packet source to the ALB's address; adding the VPN CIDR to the task security group restores the original source IP

The ALB terminates TLS, so the per-task NGINX receives plain HTTP — and location-level allow/deny directives are only evaluated on TLS-terminated server blocks; re-terminating TLS at the task's NGINX re-enables the rules

In the old topology NGINX was the edge, so each connection's source address was the real client and the allowlist worked on it. Behind an ALB, the per-task NGINX sees the load balancer's IP on every connection: 10.8.0.0/24 never matches, so deny all catches everyone — VPN included. IP filtering must move to the layer that still sees the client: an ALB listener rule with a source_ip condition (the ALB now plays the L7-edge role), or NGINX trusting X-Forwarded-For from the ALB

Cross-zone load balancing rotates requests across ALB nodes whose addresses change over time, so any IP-based allowlist behind an ALB is inherently unstable; the fix is fronting the service with a Network Load Balancer, whose static IPs can be allowlisted
explanation: The rule didn't break — its input did. NGINX allow/deny evaluates the TCP connection's source address, and moving NGINX from the edge to behind a proxy changes what that address is: the ALB opens its own connections to the task, so every request arrives 'from' the ALB. The general principle: L7 access control must live wherever the real client identity is visible — at the new edge (ALB listener rules with source_ip conditions), or downstream only via an explicitly trusted header chain (X-Forwarded-For from a proxy you control). That is exactly why, on the ECS path, VPN restrictions are ALB rules rather than task-level nginx deny blocks. The distractors attribute the failure to the wrong layers: security groups admit or drop packets but never rewrite source addresses — and if the SG were blocking, requests would time out rather than get denied responses; TLS termination changes what NGINX decrypts, not whether location rules run — allow/deny works fine on plain HTTP; and rotating node IPs are why clients use the ALB's DNS name, irrelevant to how NGINX evaluates an inbound connection's source.

question: An EC2 host serves a public app through NGINX on 443. A new management UI, bound to port 8443, must be reachable only from the VPN. One engineer wants the rule in nginx.conf — allow 10.8.0.0/24; deny all; — arguing the config is git-versioned and reviewable; another wants a Security Group inbound rule allowing 8443 from the VPN CIDR only. The requirement covers the whole port, not a path. Where does the rule belong, and why?
choices: In NGINX: the allowlist sits next to the TLS and auth configuration it complements, lives in git where changes are reviewed, and an L7 deny returns a clean 403 the client can interpret — a Security Group drop is silent and harder to debug

In both, identically: defense in depth means every access rule is enforced at every layer that can express it, so the VPN CIDR belongs in the SG and in nginx.conf — either copy alone is a single point of failure
At the NACL: it is evaluated before the Security Group, at the subnet boundary, so a VPN-only rule there blocks earliest of all — the SG proposal stops one layer too late

At the Security Group. Pick the layer by two questions: can it express the rule, and how early does it block? A whole-port restriction is exactly the L3/L4 decision an SG makes — no path awareness needed — and the SG is enforced by the AWS network fabric before the packet reaches the host, so a non-VPN client cannot even open a TCP connection: the TLS stack, the listener, and any bug in either are never exposed to internet probing. The NGINX version leaves 8443 open to the world at the network layer — every client on the internet can complete handshakes and exercise the request parser before the L7 deny fires — and it silently assumes NGINX is the process answering 8443: if the management tool listens directly, the allowlist never runs at all, the classic bypass. Reviewability is real but solvable (SGs are Terraform-managed code); NGINX earns its place for what the SG cannot express — per-path policy on ports it serves
explanation: The two gates answer different questions in series — 'can this source reach this port at all?' (SG, L3/L4) and 'what do I do with this HTTP request?' (NGINX, L7) — and the design skill is matching each rule to the earliest layer that can express it. This requirement is port-shaped: no paths, no headers, no per-request nuance, so it fits entirely within the SG's vocabulary, and placing it there means the AWS fabric drops non-VPN packets before the host's OS ever sees them. That has a security consequence beyond neatness: attack surface. Behind an SG rule, the management UI's TLS implementation and request parsing are reachable only from the VPN; behind an NGINX-only rule, they are internet-facing components that merely reject most requests after processing them. The distractors each carry a real observation with the wrong conclusion. Git-reviewability argues for infrastructure-as-code, not for the L7 layer — SGs managed by Terraform are just as reviewable, and a clean 403 for unauthorized internet clients is a feature nobody asked for. Duplicating every rule at every layer misreads defense in depth, which is about complementary gates covering each other's blind spots — mirrored copies of the same rule add drift risk (two places to update) without adding a distinct check. And the NACL, while genuinely earlier, is the stateless subnet-wide blunt instrument: it applies to every instance in the subnet and needs manual ephemeral-port handling for return traffic — the SG is the stateful, per-instance layer you actually tune, which is why it is the standing answer for instance-scoped rules.

question: A public site on EC2 (NGINX on 443, SG allowing 443 from 0.0.0.0/0) is being hammered by one abusive source range, 198.51.100.0/24, which must be blocked while the site stays open to everyone else. The instance shares its subnet with a partner integration host that must keep accepting traffic from that same range. Where can this rule actually be expressed?
choices: At the Security Group, by adding a deny rule for 198.51.100.0/24 above the existing allow for 0.0.0.0/0 — SG rules are evaluated in order, so the more specific deny wins
At the NACL, with a deny entry for 198.51.100.0/24 at a lower rule number than the allow — the only layer that both understands deny and blocks before the host

At NGINX, with deny 198.51.100.0/24; in the server block. A Security Group is allow-only with an implicit deny for everything unlisted, so 'everyone except X' is not expressible in its vocabulary at all — there is no deny rule and no ordering to exploit. A NACL does support ordered deny entries, but it applies subnet-wide, which would also cut off the partner host that must stay reachable. NGINX is the layer whose rule set has both deny and instance scope; the cost is that the connection still reaches the host and terminates TLS before being rejected, so genuinely large-scale abuse belongs at an edge built for it (WAF, CloudFront)

Nowhere on this path — because the Security Group already allows 0.0.0.0/0 on 443, an L7 deny cannot take effect on a connection the network layer has admitted; the allow must first be narrowed before any block becomes enforceable
explanation: Layer choice is constrained by two things: what a layer's rule vocabulary can express, and what blast radius its scope implies. The SG fails the first test — it is allow-only with an implicit deny for anything unlisted, so it can express 'only these sources' but never 'all sources except these'; enumerating the complement of a /24 as allow rules is both absurd and quota-bound, and there is no rule ordering to lean on because there is nothing to order against. The NACL passes the vocabulary test (ordered allow/deny entries, evaluated lowest number first) but fails the scope test in this scenario: it guards the whole subnet, so the same entry that blocks the abuser also blocks the partner host's legitimate traffic. NGINX passes both — deny exists, and the rule lives on this instance only. The tradeoff to name out loud is where the block lands in the chain: an L7 deny happens after the TCP connection and TLS handshake, so the host still pays for every rejected request, which is exactly why volumetric abuse gets pushed to a WAF or CDN upstream instead. The last option inverts how gates in series work: each layer decides independently, and a downstream deny is fully effective on traffic an upstream layer permitted — permission to reach the port is not permission to be served.

question: An ALB in public subnets forwards to EC2 instances running NGINX on 443, in an Auto Scaling group behind a warm-pool policy that recycles instances daily. The instance SG must admit only the ALB. Which inbound rule design holds up, and what is the reasoning?
choices: Allow 443 from the ALB's current private IPs as /32 entries, refreshed by a Lambda on scaling events — pinning exact addresses is the tightest possible rule, and automation keeps it from drifting

Allow 443 from the ALB's security group as the source. An SG source can be a CIDR, a prefix list, or another security group, and choosing the SG means the rule names an identity rather than an address: any ENI in the ALB's SG is admitted, whatever IP it currently holds, so node replacement and subnet expansion need no rule changes. It also makes the rule self-documenting — it states the architectural fact 'only the load-balancer tier may reach the app tier' instead of an address list that has to be re-derived to be understood
Allow 443 from the VPC CIDR — the ALB always lives inside the VPC, so this covers every node it can ever use while keeping the internet out, and it needs no maintenance as the fleet changes

Allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and enforce the ALB-only restriction in NGINX by denying any connection whose source is not an ALB node — the L7 layer sees the connection source, so the check belongs where the request is already being parsed
explanation: This is the layered model applied to tier isolation: the SG expresses 'which sources may reach this port', and the design question is how to name the source so the rule stays correct as infrastructure moves. Referencing the ALB's security group binds the rule to membership in a tier rather than to addresses, which is what makes it survive node replacement, scaling, and new subnets — the churn in this scenario is constant, and every address-based scheme is a maintenance obligation that will eventually be out of date at the worst moment. The /32 automation option chases that churn with machinery that can lag or fail, and buys nothing over the SG reference, which is atomically correct by construction. The VPC CIDR is the tempting shortcut and is the real error: it admits every workload in the VPC, so any compromised or misbehaving instance anywhere in the network can reach the app tier directly and bypass the ALB — including the listener rules and header handling the ALB is responsible for. The last option pushes an L3/L4 decision up to L7 and leaves the port internet-facing: the TLS stack and request parser become reachable from anywhere, and the check now depends on a process on the host being configured correctly rather than on the AWS fabric dropping the packet first. Match the rule to the earliest layer that can express it, and prefer identity over addresses when the addresses are not stable.
